unifyFloor.reason: user review: 'the floor half of the water tiles (and of the rock tiles, if it shows) doesn't match the plain floor tile, so each pool gets a dark speckled band around it' -- confirmed on rock too once looked for (every mixed-mask rock tile's own floor sub-area was independently AI-generated alongside its rock, so it never quite matched the canonical floor tile's exact grain/tone).
unifyFloor.tool: NEW reusable postprocess.py subcommand `unifyfloor` (with a selftest case) -- added to scripts/tiles/postprocess.py rather than a one-off script, per the request. Classifies each tile's pixels by Lab colour distance to a small palette (postprocess.py's existing build_palette, median-cut) built from a floor reference, replaces classified pixels with the SAME-POSITION pixel from the canonical (graded) floor tile, and cleans the classification mask with a small 4-connected morphology pass (reusing the existing _connected_components helper: drops floor-classified components smaller than min_speck as stray specks, fills non-floor components smaller than min_hole that don't touch the tile border as stray pinholes). Position is NOT used for classification (each tile's floor grain is independently generated) but IS used for replacement (so the floor region becomes pixel-identical to the canonical floor tile, which is what removes the halo).
unifyFloor.classifyVsPaletteRefDecoupling: unify_floor also takes optional classify_img/classify_ref params (and the CLI has --classify-img/--classify-palette-ref) so classification can be done against a DIFFERENT, tonally-matched image than the one being edited/replaced -- needed here because the water tiles were graded with a strong, water-only darkening transform BEFORE unify_floor ran, which also dragged their own floor pixels out of any floor-palette tolerance (and, on a first attempt, coincidentally INTO the graded rock floor's tolerance band, since both are similarly dark in this palette -- see selftestNote below). The fix: classify against the RAW (pre-grade) water tile using a palette built from RAW water's own pure-floor tile (fileIndex 15), then replace in the GRADED water tile with the FINAL canonical (graded rock) floor pixels. Same two-reference approach for rock: classify against the RAW rock tiles using a palette built from the RAW (seam-repaired, ungraded) floor sample, replace with the GRADED canonical floor.
unifyFloor.selftestNote: an intermediate attempt classified the (already fully-graded, deliberately darkened) water/rock tiles directly against a palette built from the FINAL graded floor -- this coincidentally misclassified most of a nearly-all-rock tile (fileIndex 0) as 'floor' (563/576px), because this biome's graded floor (L~21.7) and its graded rock's own near-black shadow tone turned out close in Lab space. Caught by inspecting the replaced-pixel-count per tile (fileIndex 0/15, which should be ~0, were 550+); fixed by decoupling classification onto the tonally-matched pre-grade images (see above). Final counts: rock fileIndex 0 and 15 both replaced 0px (correct -- no floor in a pure-rock tile, no-op on the floor tile itself); water fileIndex 0 replaced 0px, fileIndex 15 (water's own 'pure floor', never looked up in-game) replaced ~all of it; intermediate masks replaced ~144/288/427px matching their geometric floor fraction (1/4, 1/2, 3/4 of 576px) almost exactly.
unifyFloor.selftest: python3 scripts/tiles/postprocess.py selftest -- 6 new assertions: floor region replaced pixel-identical to floor_ref; upper-terrain region untouched; a 1px hole inside the floor region gets filled+replaced; a 1px stray speck inside the upper region gets dropped (left unreplaced); image size preserved; and the classify_img/classify_ref override correctly finds+replaces the floor region of an already-graded tile using a tonally-matched pre-grade classification pair. All pass.
